notes: Mandatory lifer denied Article 5(5) compensation for pre-HRA detention; HRA not retrospective per McKerr and Wilson.

enrichment.short_title: Wright v SSHD: Article 5(5) compensation and HRA retrospectivity

statutes_considered.title: Murder (Abolition of the Death Penalty) Act 1965

key_facts: Ernest Wright, a mandatory life prisoner, sought compensation under Article 5(5) for detention from July 1993 after the Secretary of State rejected a Parole Board release recommendation.
He was eventually released on licence in December 1999 after further absconsions from open conditions.
The Home Secretary refused in December 2003 and March 2004 to consider compensation, relying on pre-HRA detention and Wynne v UK.
The claim followed Richards [2004] EWHC 93 Admin but all detention here predated the HRA commencement on 2 October 2000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's refusal to consider Article 5(5) compensation; hearing limited to HRA retrospectivity after claimant conceded on that point.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no domestic HRA claim for compensation where Article 5 breaches occurred before 2 October 2000.
enrichment.ratio: Article 5(5) compensation under the HRA is parasitic on actionable Article 5 breaches after the Act came into force; the HRA is not generally retrospective and a post-Act refusal to pay cannot create a freestanding domestic remedy for pre-Act detention.
legal_issues: Whether Article 5(5) gives a freestanding right to compensation independent of pre-HRA breaches
Whether Stafford v UK and Richards have retrospective effect for pre-HRA detention
Application of McKerr and Wilson v First County Trust to Article 5(5) claims
Whether the 1993 Parole Board rejection decision was a Convention breach

In re McKerr [2004] 1 WLR 807

notes: VAT tribunal costs appeal dismissed; no perversity where tribunal made no costs order despite halving assessment after suppression findings.

enrichment.short_title: Summer Palace v Customs: VAT tribunal costs appeal after partial assessment reduction
key_facts: Summer Palace Ltd appealed a £34,483 VAT assessment for allegedly undeclared restaurant takings between 1996 and 1999.
The VAT tribunal found suppression but criticised Customs' test-purchase evidence and reduced the assessment to £17,918.
The tribunal made no order as to costs despite the appellant's partial success.
Lawrence Collins J held the no-costs decision was within discretion given suppression findings and procedural history.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 against a VAT tribunal decision on costs only.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; tribunal's refusal to award costs held neither unreasonable nor perverse.
enrichment.ratio: A VAT tribunal may make no order as to costs where the taxpayer was partly successful but guilty of suppression and the hearing history justified withholding costs; absence of reasons may be supplied by rational inference consistent with Article 6.
legal_issues: Whether refusing any costs after nearly halving the assessment was perverse
Application of CPR costs principles to VAT tribunal rule 29 discretion
Whether tribunal failure to give reasons on costs breached Article 6
Proportionality of costs award to degree of success

notes: Court sanctioned large Aviva/Norwich Union insurance business transfer scheme under FSMA Part VII after rejecting policyholder objections.

enrichment.short_title: Re Norwich Union Linked Life: sanction of Aviva insurance business transfer scheme
key_facts: Ten Aviva group life insurers sought court sanction for a scheme rationalising UK long-term business from ten companies into four.
The scheme required 4.27 million policyholder mailings and an independent expert report by Watson Wyatt.
Policyholder objector Mr Butcher and others challenged solvency margin changes, expert independence and fairness.
Lindsay J sanctioned the scheme and approved supplemental section 112 provisions as necessary to give full effect.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under FSMA Part VII for sanction of an insurance business transfer scheme with oral objections from a policyholder.
enrichment.outcome: Scheme sanctioned as fair and appropriate; supplemental provisions approved; capital reduction petition for transferor also granted.
enrichment.ratio: An IBTS may include supplemental provisions within the scheme itself or under section 112(1)(d) where necessary to carry it out; fairness is assessed scheme-wide and does not require every policyholder to benefit, provided no material disadvantage is shown on expert evidence.
legal_issues: Scope of supplemental provisions under section 112(1)(d) FSMA
Whether changes to required minimum solvency margins rendered the scheme unfair
Independence of the FSMA scheme report expert
Whether policyholders were entitled to opt out of the scheme

notes: Case stated on New Forest byelaw prosecutions; informations defective on date and time limit but continuing offence analysis allows amendment.

enrichment.short_title: Verderers of the New Forest v Young: byelaw prosecution time limits
key_facts: The Verderers prosecuted nine commoners for pasturing horses or cattle in the New Forest without paying annual marking fees under 1999 byelaws.
Informations alleged offences on or before 30 April 2002 but were laid in October/November 2002 and evidence showed depasturing in May–July.
A deputy district judge wrongly held all informations out of time under section 127, then purported to set aside that ruling after Marren v Dawson Bentley.
Collins J held most October informations were in time, section 142 did not apply, and the magistrate could not reopen her substantive ruling.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Divisional Court appeal by case stated on jurisdiction, time limits and power to amend informations for New Forest byelaw offences.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted on undertaking to amend informations to allege dates when animals were actually seen depastured.
enrichment.ratio: Depasturing without payment is a continuing offence for limitation purposes; time runs from the date alleged in the information, and defective date averments may be amended unless fundamental, but magistrates cannot reopen a final jurisdictional ruling under section 142 where no conviction occurred.
legal_issues: Whether byelaw offences were continuing offences for section 127 purposes
Calculation of six-month limitation under Marren v Dawson Bentley
Whether magistrates could set aside an erroneous out-of-time ruling without section 142
Whether informations could be amended to correct dates of alleged depasturing

notes: Permission to appeal refused in long-running mortgagee/receiver negligence claim over Black offer and farm management.

enrichment.short_title: Lloyds Bank v Cassidy: permission to appeal on receiver duty and Black offer
key_facts: Michael Cassidy counterclaimed that Lloyds Bank and Touche Ross receivers breached duties by rejecting a September 1991 rescue offer and mismanaging his mortgaged farms.
After a 21-day trial Judge Langan found only £9,147.90 damages for 1992 harvest mismanagement, halved for partnership/trustee reasons.
The Black offer of about £480,000 was held not obviously favourable against total indebtedness near £590,000 and unlikely to complete.
Clarke LJ refused permission on all grounds including alleged transcript procedural unfairness.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal application for permission to appeal after strike-out appeal succeeded and full trial before HHJ Langan.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; no real prospect of success on Black offer, 1993 sowing, damages or procedural points.
enrichment.ratio: Once mortgagees or receivers decide to sell, they may reject outline proposals that are not obviously favourable and are unlikely to complete; receiver duties on sale timing and pre-sale works are limited and bad-faith claims fail where decisions were objectively justified.
legal_issues: Whether receivers owed duties to accept an obviously favourable offer after deciding to sell
Whether rejection of the Black offer breached Palk v Mortgage Services duties
Whether receivers were in breach for not sowing the 1993 harvest
Whether damages for harvest loss should have been awarded in full rather than halved
linked_authorities: Palk v Mortgage Services Funding plc [1993] Ch 330
Silven Properties Ltd v Royal Bank of Scotland plc [2004] EWCA Civ 846

notes: Telecom mast appeal dismissed; inspector could treat police and railway alternative sites as unavailable without County Court code-power analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Leger-Davey v FSS: telecom mast alternatives and code power
key_facts: Orange appealed Winchester City Council's refusal of prior approval for an 11.79m mast at Byron Avenue near a school.
An inspector allowed the appeal after finding police HQ and railway station alternatives unavailable despite technical superiority.
Residents argued the inspector should have assessed Schedule 2 paragraph 5 code powers to compel landowners to grant mast rights.
Sullivan J dismissed judicial review; the Court of Appeal upheld the inspector's approach to landowner objections.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal planning appeal from Sullivan J's refusal to quash an inspector's decision granting prior approval for a telecommunications mast.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; inspector entitled to treat alternative sites as unachievable having regard to landowners' objections without detailed paragraph 5 analysis.
enrichment.ratio: PPG8 requires consideration of alternative mast sites, but an applicant need not apply to the County Court under the telecommunications code or prove it would fail; planning authorities may weigh landowners' refusal and public-service objections as material considerations when asking whether a site is the best location.
legal_issues: Whether alternative sites were a material planning consideration under PPG8
Proper use of Schedule 2 paragraph 5 Telecommunications Act code powers in planning decisions
Whether the inspector erred in treating police and Network Rail sites as unavailable
Whether the inspector should have second-guessed County Court paragraph 5(3) balancing

notes: Suspended committal of mother for defying contact order upheld; seven-day sentence appropriate for persistent breach.

enrichment.short_title: Re S (a child): appeal against suspended committal for contact breach
key_facts: Long-running contact disputes between parents over their six-year-old daughter began in June 2002.
The mother agreed to contact in August 2004 but then persistently breached the order despite a penal notice.
Judge Finnerty committed her to seven days' imprisonment suspended on condition she comply with Saturday contact.
The mother failed to attend the committal hearing and expressed contempt for the court's authority.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against a suspended committal order for breach of a child contact order with related stay of further county court enforcement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; suspended seven-day committal upheld as a proper exercise of discretion to enforce contact.
enrichment.ratio: Where a parent persistently and defiantly breaches a contact order backed by a penal notice, a short suspended committal is a legitimate last-resort means of upholding court authority and promoting compliance in the child's interests.
legal_issues: Whether committal was a proper exercise of discretion
Whether suspended imprisonment was proportionate
Role of mediation and community support after dismissal of appeal

notes: Child Abduction Act convictions quashed; detention after foster parents lost control was section 2(1)(b) not charged section 2(1)(a).

enrichment.short_title: Foster v DPP: Child Abduction Act removal versus keeping out of control
key_facts: Two men took a 15-year-old girl from Meadowhall to Sheffield, plied her with drink and hid her when police searched on 2 March 2003.
On 1 March they believed she was 16 and thus had a section 3(b) belief defence; police told them her true age after midnight.
They lied to officers and induced her to remain hidden in the attic, detaining her away from foster parents who had lost control.
They were charged under section 2(1)(a) for detention so as to remove from lawful control on 2 March and convicted.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeals by case stated from magistrates' court convictions under section 2(1)(a) Child Abduction Act 1984.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed and convictions quashed; acts on 2 March 2003 kept the child out of lawful control under section 2(1)(b), not remove under (a).
enrichment.ratio: Section 2(1)(a) requires taking or detaining a child who is then in another's lawful control so as to remove that control; once lawful control is lost, subsequent detention only keeps the child out of control under section 2(1)(b), a separate offence not charged here; removal means substitution of authority not geographical movement.
legal_issues: Whether operative removal could occur after the child was already out of foster parents' control
Distinction between section 2(1)(a) and section 2(1)(b)
Meaning of 'detains' including inducement under section 3(c)
Mens rea following Mousir, Leather and Owens

notes: School admissions appeal panel judicial review; Beatson J allowed claim for inadequate reasons on guarantee and transport issues despite infant class size limits.

enrichment.short_title: C v Nottinghamshire admissions panel: inadequate reasons on school appeal
key_facts: Ms C appealed after Nottinghamshire refused her younger daughter A a place at All Hallows C of E Primary because the admissions limit was reached and other pupils had higher priority.
Grounds included an elder daughter already at the school, difficulty transporting children to two schools, and an alleged headmaster guarantee that A would get a place.
The appeal panel dismissed the appeal by standard form letter citing infant class size prejudice and the limited statutory grounds for allowing appeals.
Ex post facto explanations did not address how the panel dealt with the guarantee dispute or transport concerns.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an admissions appeal panel decision; permission initially refused on the papers but granted on renewal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed for failure to give adequate reasons; section 39 anonymity order made; claimant denied costs for non-compliance with the judicial review pre-action protocol.
enrichment.ratio: Even where infant class size limits restrict the grounds on which an appeal panel may allow an appeal, a standard form dismissal letter is insufficient when significant factual issues such as an alleged guarantee of admission and transport difficulties require individual treatment; reasons must explain why the appellant's particular circumstances did not outweigh prejudice arguments.
legal_issues: Whether an admissions appeal panel gave legally adequate reasons under regulation 1.8
Whether standard form letters suffice when specific factual issues are raised
Whether infant class size statutory constraints reduce the duty to give reasons
Whether ex post facto witness statements and solicitor letters cure inadequate decision letters

notes: SENDIST section 11 appeal adjourned so tribunal could address whether chairman's private preparation notes may be relied on.

enrichment.short_title: F v Kent CC: adjournment on SENDIST chairman's private notes
key_facts: Mr and Mrs F appealed a SENDIST determination on 27 July 2004 about special educational provision for their 11-year-old son J.
Grounds included mishandling of expert evidence, inadequate reasons, and insufficient specificity of statement amendments.
Chairman's notes obtained shortly before hearing included seven pages marked preparation before hearing notes began on page 8.
Claimants wished to rely on preparation notes; the court was not satisfied disclosure was intentional or that their status was settled.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 from a SENDIST decision.
enrichment.outcome: Hearing adjourned to 20 December; SENDIST invited to make submissions by 13 December on whether the court may or should consider the chairman's private preparation notes; costs reserved.
enrichment.ratio: Where a tribunal chairman's private preparation notes are disclosed and may contain material relevant to an appeal, the court should not determine their admissibility without giving the tribunal opportunity to make representations on whether such notes may be relied upon.
legal_issues: Whether a tribunal chairman's private preparation notes may be used on a section 11 appeal
Whether inadvertent disclosure of preparation notes should be treated as intentional
Appropriate procedure when novel evidential issues arise on a listed SENDIST appeal
